key_points: EBUS-TBNA is guideline-recommended as the initial approach for mediastinal staging in lung cancer.
EBUS-TBMCB provides larger, intact samples and can improve diagnostic yield, particularly for benign and uncommon entities; safety is generally acceptable.
A combined approach (EBUS-TBNA + cryobiopsy) can enhance adequacy for molecular/immunologic testing without increasing complications.
Transesophageal mediastinal cryobiopsy is an alternative route when tracheal access is not feasible.

clinical_procedures.name: Indications and contraindications for EBUS-TBMCB
steps: Indications: at least one mediastinal lesion with short-axis ≥1 cm on thoracic imaging; newly discovered mediastinal lesions; clinical symptoms needing biopsy to establish etiology.
Contraindications: severe cardiopulmonary disease, coagulation disorders, intolerance to anesthesia or endoscopic procedures, psychiatric disorders, severe neurosis.
notes: Ensure necessary preoperative labs and imaging (cardiac ultrasound or CTA when indicated).

clinical_procedures.name: Anesthesia for EBUS-TBMCB
steps: Supine position; upper airway topical anesthesia with 2% lidocaine.
Conscious sedation with IV midazolam and fentanyl.
Administer oxygen 1–2 L/min; increase if SpO2 <90%.
Continuous monitoring of vital signs and pulse oximetry.

clinical_procedures.name: Systematic EBUS examination
steps: Insert EBUS bronchoscope via nasal route (oral route if nasal passage unsuitable).
Sequentially examine mediastinal and hilar stations per Mountain-Dressler map.
Use Doppler to assess blood supply; measure long and short axes.
Select the most suspicious lesion with relatively lower biopsy risk as target.

clinical_procedures.name: Creating a window on the airway wall
steps: Under real-time ultrasound, advance a high-frequency needle-knife via the working channel.
Make a 2–3 mm cut on airway wall adjacent to the target lesion.
Advance into the lesion under ultrasound visualization, avoiding areas with abundant blood flow or massive necrosis; measure insertion depth; withdraw knife.
notes: Laser thermal ablation has been reported for windowing.
Alternative approach: insert cryoprobe through the puncture tract created by TBNA needle.

clinical_procedures.name: Cryobiopsy sampling
steps: Advance an appropriate cryoprobe through the window into the lesion under real-time ultrasound.
Activate with nitrous oxide for ~7 s; gently extract probe with frozen specimen attached.
Release specimen by thawing in saline; fix in formalin; send to pathology.
notes: Cryoprobe yields intact samples with greater volume compared to TBNA needle or forceps.

clinical_procedures.name: Postprocedure check and follow-up
steps: Inspect airway for hemorrhage; apply topical procoagulants as needed.
Obtain chest X-ray or other imaging within 24 hours to detect pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum, or mediastinitis.
Follow-up at 24 hours to record symptoms; consider a second follow-up at 1 month.
notes: Severe adverse events include Grade 3–4 bleeding, oversedation requiring ventilatory support or reversal, pneumothorax with persistent air leak (>5 days), unplanned readmission, ICU transfer within 48 h, and death.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Guide aspiration of mediastinal lymph nodes or masses for histological and cytological analysis; detecting and staging mediastinal diseases.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Uses ultrasound imaging during bronchoscopy to guide aspiration of lymph nodes or masses in the mediastinum.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Offers comparable diagnostic efficiency for detecting and staging mediastinal diseases.
limitations: Small tissue amounts may lack sufficient cells or architecture
hindering definitive diagnosis and molecular testing.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration (EBUS-TBNA) is a minimally invasive procedure that uses ultrasound imaging during bronchoscopy to guide the aspiration of lymph nodes or masses

diagnostic_approaches.name: Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial mediastinal cryobiopsy (EBUS-TBMCB)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Obtain larger, intact mediastinal tissue samples; enhance diagnostic yield for mediastinal diseases and molecular diagnosis.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Under real-time EBUS guidance, create an airway wall window with a high-frequency needle-knife; insert cryoprobe into lesion to freeze and extract tissue; thaw and fix specimen.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Demonstrated higher overall diagnostic yield versus EBUS-TBNA; generally safe with minor adverse events.
limitations: No conclusive evidence regarding impact of cryoprobe diameter on diagnostic accuracy.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Sampling and diagnosis of mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes and lesions; patients with newly discovered mediastinal lesions or relevant symptoms requiring biopsy.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: endobronchial ultrasound-guided trans-bronchial mediastinal cryobiopsy (EBUS-TBMCB) has been introduced as an alternative for mediastinal lymph node sampling.

problems_observed.finding: Guidelines recommend EBUS-TBNA as the initial technique for mediastinal staging, but it often yields insufficient tissue for full histopathologic and molecular workup.
problems_observed.details: Small tissue/cell yield can hinder definitive diagnosis of benign mediastinal disease and uncommon tumors, limiting diagnostic accuracy and molecular testing.
problems_observed.reference: [1,2,18] for guideline recommendations; limitations of EBUS-TBNA noted in [7,20].

problems_observed.finding: Emerging evidence supports adjunctive EBUS-TBMCB with higher diagnostic yield, but this is not yet reflected in guideline recommendations favoring needle-based techniques.
problems_observed.details: A randomized controlled trial (n=197) showed EBUS-TBMCB had a higher overall diagnostic yield than EBUS-TBNA, particularly improving diagnosis of benign diseases and uncommon tumors, with only minor adverse events reported.

guideline_adherence.implication: Strict adherence to needle-based first-line staging (EBUS-TBNA) may result in under-evaluation for cases requiring larger tissue architecture or molecular profiling, potentially delaying or compromising diagnosis and treatment selection. Incorporating EBUS-TBMCB as a complementary approach can increase diagnostic yield and improve access to molecular testing while maintaining safety.

technology_and_technique.summary: A 2021 randomized controlled trial (n=197) showed EBUS-TBMCB achieved higher overall diagnostic yield than EBUS-TBNA, with particular improvement for benign diseases and uncommon tumors. EBUS-TBMCB also improved adequacy for subsequent molecular testing. Adverse events were minor.

Traditional surgical mediastinoscopy and related surgeries carry a 2–3% risk of serious complications (mediastinal infection, pneumothorax, esophageal injury) and higher costs. Needle-based approaches (e.g., EBUS-TBNA) offer comparable diagnostic efficiency with lower invasiveness and complication risk; guidelines recommend needle-based techniques as first-line for lung cancer staging.

technology_and_technique.topic: EBUS-TBMCB procedural technique and performance tips
technology_and_technique.summary: Key steps: preprocedural thin-section chest CT; real-time linear EBUS to precisely locate target; perform TBNA then create a bronchial window using a high-frequency needle-knife; insert cryoprobe through the window into the node under continuous ultrasound guidance; obtain larger, intact samples; perform postprocedure check. Tips to improve performance and safety: keep real-time EBUS visualization to avoid vessels, create the airway wall window adjacent to the target, use the cryoprobe to maximize sample volume/architecture, and confirm hemostasis post-sampling.

Across reported experience including the RCT, EBUS-TBMCB demonstrated a good safety profile with only minor adverse events. It provides larger tissue samples while maintaining safety comparable to needle-based bronchoscopic approaches.

Consider EBUS-TBMCB when EBUS-TBNA yields insufficient cellularity/tissue architecture for definitive histopathology or molecular testing, particularly for benign mediastinal disease and uncommon tumors. It is anticipated to complement, not replace, EBUS-TBNA in staging and diagnosis.

A transesophageal approach to mediastinal cryobiopsy is described as an alternative access route using similar ultrasound guidance and cryoprobe sampling principles for selected mediastinal targets. Specific yield and safety percentages were not provided in the excerpt.

points: Guidelines endorse EBUS-TBNA as initial mediastinal staging; however, limited tissue may restrict definitive diagnosis and molecular testing.
EBUS-TBMCB provides larger, intact specimens and improves diagnostic yield, especially in benign and uncommon disorders, with generally minor adverse events.
A combined strategy (EBUS-TBNA + cryobiopsy) increases diagnostic yield and sample adequacy; a transesophageal route is feasible when tracheal access is not.
Further prospective data are needed to refine indications, optimize technique, and confirm safety across settings.
